questions.q: What does “start big, but small” mean in the summary?
a: Aim for a large share of a small market
Launch with a big budget in a tiny office
Start with many products for a few customers
Grow quickly by entering every market at once
questions.why: Lesson 1 says most startups chase a tiny slice of a huge market, while the better move is dominating a small one.

questions.q: Which early example of starting locally does the summary give?
a: Facebook limited at first to Harvard students
Amazon selling only books to begin with
Google launching in every country at once
Apple selling only to schools
questions.why: Lesson 1 pairs Facebook’s Harvard launch with Uber’s early focus on San Francisco.

a: A free version of the product with optional paid upgrades
A free trial that ends after thirty days
A product paid for entirely by advertising
A discount offered to the first customers
questions.why: Lesson 2 defines freemium as free basic use with an optional upgrade to more features.

questions.q: When does freemium tend to fail, according to the summary?
a: When the product is complicated and takes time to learn
When the free version has too many features
When the company charges too little for upgrades
When the product is too easy for people to use
questions.why: Lesson 2 says people will not invest weeks learning software they did not pay for, citing ConvertKit as an example.

questions.q: Why build a free tool alongside your main product?
a: It draws in potential customers by solving a pressing problem
It replaces the need for a paid product entirely
It guarantees that investors will fund the company
It keeps competitors from copying your idea
questions.why: Lesson 3 says tools like a headline analyzer or Pablo attract an audience and can feed a freemium model.
